title: Not Everything Needs an LLM
lede: PostHog's Jina Yoon describes where the company uses decision models, which return a typed answer with a calibrated probability, in place of a full LLM call.

points: Two narrow yes/no checks screen session summaries for personal data, and 98.7% of them skip the Gemini rewrite entirely.
Thresholds follow the cost of each mistake: 0.4 for PII, where a miss stores personal data, and 0.85 for a Slack bot answering untagged messages.
A single choice question routes Slack bot requests to the cheapest model likely to succeed first time, using a short note per model.
Reranking embedding search results by a decision model's match score improved ranking quality by about 25% on 20 queries.
Chained multi-step judgments and open-ended ranking, such as triaging PR review findings, did not work and stay with LLMs.

points.text: One commenter doubts decision-model rerankers, arguing a trained reranker is easy to build, already calibrated, and smaller and faster.
Using one as a model router drew doubt, since newer models will postdate the router and it only sees a short blurb about each.
Others blame managers who reach for LLMs where a regex, a function or a plain algorithm would do.
Some see little beyond structured JSON output, which has existed for years; a reply says the real gain is speed.
